intro.title: React
intro.intro: React re-runs your component function far more often than most people expect, and far less often than they fear. Almost every confusing React bug comes down to one of three questions: how many times did this render, which closure did that callback capture, and did this element keep its identity across the update? Each challenge below is a short component you can trace on paper. Assume React 18 or later, and that effects run in a real browser unless the question says otherwise.

questions.title: Twice on Purpose

hints.text: StrictMode in development does two separate things on mount: it invokes the component function an extra time, and it runs the effect, immediately tears it down, and runs it again.
Both counters end up with the same value, and it is not one. `cleanups`, the counter the question does not ask about, ends on 1 — the teardown between the two effect runs.

questions.title: Four Updates, One Render

hints.text: Walk the queue with a running value that starts at 0. Each of the four entries either overwrites that running value with a fixed number, or transforms it.
`n` is 0 for the whole handler, so the third call overwrites the running value with 2 and discards everything the second call computed. Only the fourth call's transformation survives.

questions.title: Three Dependency Arrays

hints.text: There are four commits in total: the mount plus three updates. Count how many of those four each effect participates in.

The no-dependency effect re-runs on every commit. The empty-array one only ever runs at mount. The `[count]` one runs at mount and then only when `count` differs from the previous render — the third update leaves it alone.

questions.title: The Interval That Forgot

hints.text: The interval callback in TickerA closes over the `count` from the render in which the effect ran. That effect never re-runs, so that captured value never changes, no matter how many times the component re-renders.

TickerA's callback computes the same fixed sum on every tick; after the first tick the state stops changing, so React bails out of further renders. TickerB's updater receives the current value each time, so it climbs by one per tick.

questions.title: Keys by Index

hints.text: Before the update, the typed text lives in the DOM node rendered under key `0`. Ask which name occupies key `0` after the prepend.

`defaultValue` is only used when the input is first created. Since key `0` already existed, React updates that same DOM node's sibling text and leaves the input untouched — so the typed text stays at the top of the list while the names all slide down one position.

questions.title: Memo, Defeated

hints.text: An arrow function written in the JSX is a brand new object on every render of the parent, and two distinct function objects are never `Object.is`-equal even when the source text matches.

Under ParentA the memo comparison fails on every update, so the child renders once per parent render — mount plus three updates. Under ParentB the prop is the same object every time, so after the mount the child never renders again.

questions.title: Context Slips Past Memo

hints.text: Start at the component that owns the state — it always re-renders. Then ask, for each component below it, whether React reaches it by walking the tree or by waking it up as a context subscriber.

`Toolbar` bails out on its unchanged (empty) props, which would normally spare everything beneath it — but React schedules a re-render directly on every component that read the context whose value changed. Only one component below the memo boundary calls `useContext`, and its sibling is untouched.

questions.title: Bottom Up, Top Down

hints.text: Both renders happen before either effect does — React finishes the whole render pass and commits the DOM, then flushes effects afterwards.
The render pass goes outside-in: parent first, then child. The effect flush goes inside-out: the deepest component's effect runs first, and the parent's runs last.

questions.title: Cleanup Before Setup

hints.text: Only the update matters, not the mount. Both dependency arrays changed, so both effects are torn down and both are re-created.

All of the destroy work happens first, then all of the create work — and each pass visits the effects in the order they were declared in the component body, so the effect written first leads both passes.

questions.title: A New Component Every Render

hints.text: Count the renders of `Search` first: the mount, plus one per keystroke. Then ask how many of those renders produce an element type React considers unchanged.
None of them match — every render redefines the inner function, so every render is a fresh mount of the subtree. The count is therefore one per render of the parent, and there are four of those.
